- `SUM` and `PROD` are generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`. Write the element type wherever generators stand in brackets, also where the generators, the body or a declared type fix it: `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. The checker refuses a call without it (ledger row 731). Walk runs such a call at its value's declared type, or else at the join of its elements' run-time types. An empty `SUM` with no static argument written and no declared type gives the integer 0, and an empty `PROD` the integer 1, whatever the body's type (ledger row 716). With a static argument written that is not a number type, such as a user group, an empty or filtered `SUM` ends in `CastError` (ledger row 436).
- An indexed type's index parameter is bounded by `Index` (`revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects"). `BoundedRange[\I\]` cannot take the bound, because the open range `(:)` stays a range over `Any` (P-56). So its `atMost(n: I): FullRange[\I\]` has the condition `where { I extends Index }`, which each call must meet (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`). A type whose static parameter is a range's index type takes the bound too, as `UniformDistribution[\T extends Index\]` over a `FullRange[\T\]` (`Library/Random.fsi`).
- An array's `fill` takes a value, and its `tabulate` a function of the index: `array[\ZZ32\](4).fill(0)`, `array[\ZZ32\](4).tabulate(fn (i:ZZ32):ZZ32 => 10 i)`. The factories that take a function are `tabulatedArray1` to `tabulatedArray3` and `tabulatedVector`.

## Designing a change

- Put each extension into this library, outside the compiler's files. This includes an extension that only the model program needs.
- Fix a gap in the library, not by a workaround in the program that meets it. Take the design from the library's practice as well as from the specification's text. If the two disagree, do as `specification.md`, "When the text and an implementation disagree", says.
- If a rule of the language or the checker refuses the way that you want, find how the library writes that kind of thing. Do the same. The checker's refusals of this library reach you through your brief, or through a run of the count stage (`compiler.md`): `fortress typecheck` checks against the compiler's prelude.
- When you add a method, make it dotted or functional as its family in the library does. If the family shows no practice, follow the team's proposal, which no program can import (`Library/incomplete/Collection.fss`): an updater, a getter or a setter, indexing included, is dotted, and every other method is functional.
- A new functional method reserves its name in every program that imports the library. The phase that binds names then refuses each program that names a variable or a parameter after it: "Variable even is already declared."
- A `fail` without a static argument has the result type `Any`. Where it must have a type, write the static argument, as `strToInt` calls `fail[\ZZ32\]`.
- A dotted method shadows a top-level function of the same name (`overloading.tex`, "Principles of Overloading").
- In an api, declare each top-level function and each member of a trait or object at the header that the component gives it. A function's header is its name, its static parameters with their bounds, its modifiers, its `throws` clause, its parameters' modifiers and types, and its return type. The parameters' names and a `where` clause do not count. In the cases below, change the component's header to the api's, not the api's to the component's. The examples are in `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` and `Library/FortressLibrary.fss`.
  - The member's body already answers the api's type. `RR64`'s `opr |\self/|`, `opr |/self\|` and `truncate` answer `ZZ64`, because they call `Float`'s natives, which answer `ZZ64` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:184-191`).
  - The api cannot name the component's type. `Array2`'s and `Array3`'s `bounds` and `zeroIndices` answered types of `RangeInternals`, which depends on this api. They now answer the api's `CompactFullRange` types, which those types extend.
  - The api's type is wider, and the overrides and bodies use only that type. `DelegatedIndexed`'s `generator` answers the api's `Generator[\E\]`, as `FlatString`'s override does.

  In the api, write `abstract` on each member that the component leaves without a body.
- The compiled checker's export check matches an api member with a component member of the same name and header. It matches a field by its name, its type and its modifiers other than `var`. It also requires a component member for each api member written `abstract`, at the api's header, with a body or without one. Each entry of the check's error names a trait or object and only its first member that differs. After you fix that member, check again to see the next.
- A new overload can make walk refuse every program at load. `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists what walk refuses.
- A new native is a Java class under `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`interpreter.md`, "Natives"), so it is an edit of walk's Java too.
- `interpreter.md`, "The model program", says how to check microGPT under walk.

# The compiled checker, the code generator and the run time

**count stage**
: Script that runs the compiled checker over the interpreter's library, on the `FortressLibrary` component and the apis that it imports, and prints the errors in a table: `explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh`. Its total is the checker count.

The code of this area is in these directories:

- `scala_src/typechecker/`: the type checker, in Scala.
- `compiler/`: the disambiguator, the desugarers, overloading, `codegen/`, `NamingCzar` and `OverloadSet`.
- `runtimeSystem/`: `InstantiatingClassloader`, tasks and transactions.

The phases' names in the code are parse, PREDISAMBIGUATEDESUGAR, DISAMBIGUATE, GRAMMAR, PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR, INTEGERLITERALFOLDING, TYPECHECK, DESUGAR, OVERLOADREWRITE and CODEGEN.

## What the two paths share

After the phases, each path has its own code for these:

- Values: walk's `interpreter/evaluator/values/` (`FInt`, `FFloat`), and the compiled `compiler/runtimeValues/` (`FZZ32`, `FRR64`).
- Number natives: walk's `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`Int.java`, `Long.java`), and the compiled `nativeHelpers/` (`simpleIntArith.java`).
- Dispatch: walk searches at run time, in `OverloadedFunction`. The compiled path calls a dispatch method that `OverloadSet` generates.
- The run: `fortress run` starts a second JVM (`bin/run`), which never enters `Shell.java`.

The phases differ too: walk turns off some desugarings that the compiled path runs (`interpreter.md`, "Where a fix of walk belongs"). A fix of one of those desugarers changes only the compiled path.

## The compiler's prelude, until the switch-over

The compiled path uses the compiler's own prelude: `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` and `Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss`. `Library/CompilerSystem.fss` is the compiled path's `System`.

Do not add a declaration to the three prelude files: they are deleted at the switch-over. Their tests stay.

## What the compiled path cannot compile yet

For a construct that it cannot compile yet, the code generator calls `sayWhat` or throws another `CompilerError`. Such a call or throw is a code-generator wall. The code generator has no case for these constructs:

- `label` and `exit`, `spawn`, and `atomic` used as an expression;
- a local function declaration, and an object expression;
- an array literal, such as `[1 2 3]`.

It also refuses a function, method, object or trait declaration with a `where` clause of its own, and a function or method with a contract (`requires`, `ensures`, `invariant`). It compiles a declaration whose `extends` entry has a `where` clause. The disambiguator, which both paths run, drops a trait's or object's contract, so the code generator never sees one, and walk does not check one either (ledger row 781). It refuses a function or method with a modifier other than `getter`, `setter`, `io`, `private` and `abstract`, such as `override` (ledger row 650).

The compiler's prelude has no array types, only `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`. Its `for` loops, comprehensions and reductions work over `ZZ32` ranges only. Its reductions give a `ZZ32` or a `String`.

Until the switch-over, a compiled test uses none of these. If a test needs one, write it as an `XXX` test that names the wall (`tests-writing.md`).

## What the code generator does

`SKILL.md`, "The compiled run time", gives the jars, the dispatch methods, the templates and the boxed numbers.

- It emits no primitive `double` arithmetic.
- The class loader rewrites a template's bytes with ASM. The emitted classfiles stay at version 1.6, because this rewriting keeps no stack-map frames. Do not raise the version.
- The `value` modifier has no effect on the representation.
- An array of `RR64` values is to be stored as an unboxed `double[]`. The code generator does not build it yet (`SKILL.md`, "The compiled run time"). If your task touches how arrays are stored, print the two POSITIONS entries on arrays first (about 2 KB):

      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'positions:array is stored as' 'positions:array design'

## The run time

- The class loader is `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java`. The revival has changed it for sizes and for the lock on a class's first load (ledger row 417). Before you investigate a failure while a class loads, read ledger rows 408 and 559, which name it (`records.md`, "Reading the record").
- The compiled code keeps each mutable variable in a cell (`compiler/runtimeValues/MutableFValue.java`). Before each read and write of the cell, the generated code asks `BaseTask.inATransaction()` (`runtimeSystem/`). Inside an `atomic` block, the access goes through the transaction. So the transaction tracks the variables that the block touches.

## Natives

`import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{...}` in a `.fss` file binds static Java methods over plain Java values.

The wrapper generator wraps every method of a class that it is given, the private methods too. If a type has no Fortress counterpart, it fails the whole import. So give every method of a helper class a signature that maps to Fortress, also a private method.

content.content:
## Traps of the compiled path

- An api and the component that implements it must have the same name. The linker looks for a component with the api's own name. If there is none, the link fails ("Could not find an implementation for API"), and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError`.
- The compiled dispatch ignores the contravariance of a parameter of arrow type. The property `fortress.disable.contravariance` is true by default, so `OverloadSet` passes no variance. The team turned it off in 2012 (`c35aac139`). If a compiled call with function arguments picks another declaration than walk does, look here first.
- A clean link does not prove that every call has its method. A call of a functional method of an object that a trait's `comprises` clause lists dies at run time with `NoSuchMethodError` on a value whose static type is the object. An example is `num(R)`, where `trait Q comprises { R }` declares `abstract num(self): ZZ32` and `object R extends Q` gives its body. Call it through a value typed as the trait, as `q: Q = R` and then `num(q)` (ledger row 815).

## The checker's gaps

`revival-changes.md` gives the rules. This section gives where the checker applies them, and where it does not yet.

- Overloads: in its test of whether two domains exclude each other, the checker puts the meet of a static parameter's declared bounds in the parameter's place where the parameter is a whole parameter type, an element of a tuple or a member of an intersection or union (P-157). Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays. The paths differ on `tint[\T extends Red\](x: Box[\T\])` beside `tint[\T extends Blue\](x: Box[\T\])`, where `Red`, `Blue` and `Box` are objects. The checker refuses it, because `Box[\Bottom\]` lies in both domains, and walk loads it. No decision says which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 786).
- A `where` clause's constraint: the checker checks a function's or functional method's constraint on its own static parameters at the call. At a dotted call, a candidate is not applicable where the receiver's static argument breaks the method's constraint. A trait's or object's own constraint is checked where its type is used, also at a constructor call; only the checker reads it, and the code generator refuses such a declaration (ledger row 701). A `where`-clause variable is a static parameter of the function's arrow type, inferred at the call. The checker does not yet check these, and no ledger row holds the first two:
  - at a dotted call, a constraint whose bound names the method's own static parameters or a `where`-clause variable;
  - at a type's use, a constraint whose bound names a `where`-clause variable;
  - a static argument written at a top-level call, against its parameter's bound (ledger row 470).
- Imports: `import A.{...}`, with the three dots written, imports every name of `A`. The overloading check also reads `A`'s declarations of a name that the component imports by name from another api. So `import A.{...}` beside `import B.{ pick }`, where both apis declare `pick(x: P)`, is refused: 'There are multiple declarations of pick' (ledger row 813). Leave the name out of the whole import, as `import A.{...} except { pick }`.
- An `except` clause leaves out each identifier that it lists, on both paths. The compiled path does not leave out an infix operator that it lists. So where a component lists `-` in `except` and declares its own `-` at the api's parameter types, the code generator stops. Walk runs the component's own `-` (ledger row 814).
- Conditional extension: the condition holds while the checker checks the `extends` entry itself, an object's value parameters and every member. It does not hold for the other `extends` entries, the static parameters, the declaration's own `where` clause, and the `excludes` and `comprises` clauses. The checker lets a member that it checked under the condition be called where the condition fails (ledger row 773).
- A `comprises` clause that lists a type at a `where`-clause variable, as `NatParam comprises { N[\n\] } where [\ nat n \]` or `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`: at a call, the checker gives the variable a fresh size or type, equal only to itself. Two values passed in one call get two. A fresh type is bounded by the binding and by the clause's constraints. The variable is in scope in the trait, except in its `extends` and `excludes` clauses. The checker gives no fresh type where it meets the trait as a supertype of another type. A program that declares such a trait does not compile: the code generator refuses the trait's `where` clause (ledger row 701). Where a generic type that the clause lists, as `List[\E\]`, gives the body of a member of the trait, the code generator crashes before it refuses the clause: 'E is not in the kind env' (ledger row 812). Departures: a fresh type also under a function type's result (ledger row 751), none for an extender that the clause does not list (ledger row 752), and a crash at a call, from outside the trait, of a member whose type names the variable (ledger row 756).

## The `fortress` commands

`Shell.java` dispatches `bin/fortress <command>`.

- To see what an early phase makes of a program, stop after that phase: `parse` (a syntax check), `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` or `typecheck`.
- `unparse` prints the syntax tree back as Fortress source. Use it to see what a desugaring made.
- `link` links a compiled component (the `link` step of a compiled `.test` file). `api` writes a component's api. `test` runs a program's `test` declarations under walk.
- The command chooses the library. Walk and `test` call `Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()`. Every other command calls `useCompilerLibraries()`. Each call points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` to its prelude, and sets the desugaring switches.

## Running

    cd ProjectFortress
    # after an ant compileAll that started the caches again: the library order (build-and-caches.md)
    ../bin/fortress compile <path>/P.fss
    ../bin/fortress run P [args]

A small program compiles in about 5 s and runs in about 1 s.

- A crash of the checker prints one line and hides the Java stack. To see the stack, put `-debug stacktrace` before the file: `../bin/fortress compile -debug stacktrace <path>/P.fss`.
- A failed compile of a program leaves a 0-byte jar in `bytecode_cache/`. A run of the program then prints "Could not load P" and "Resource not found". Read the compile's error instead: it gives the cause.

## Before an edit

Two notes under `explorations/coordinator/map/` help you find where a fix belongs. Both date from September 2026, so a status or a line number in them can be stale. Before you rely on a status, read the ledger rows that it cites. Before you rely on a line number, grep for the method's name.

- Before you add or fix a language feature, print its row of the feature table. WORD names the feature, such as `spawn`, `coercion` or `typecase`. A row is about 1 KB. It names the feature's section of the specification, its parser rule, checker class, walk site, code-generator site, prelude declaration and ledger rows.

      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:spec-to-implementation.md#Feature by feature@WORD'

- If your edit is in one phase, and you need what runs before and after it on each path, print that phase's section. Name the section by its number and the first word of its title. A section is 1 to 3 KB. B.1 is the phase list, B.4 disambiguation, B.5 desugaring, B.6 type checking, B.7 overloading, B.10 the caches, B.11 the run time and B.12 the natives.

      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:modules-and-phases.md#B.5 Desugaring'

- Before you change the text of a diagnostic, grep the `.test` files for it. A `.test` file can pin a whole diagnostic with `compile_err_equals`, its `file:line:column` included. `grep -l 'TEXT' ProjectFortress/*tests/*.test`, with words of the diagnostic as TEXT, lists the files that pin it. Update each of those in the same commit. A line that you add to or remove from a compiler test program moves the pinned spans below it.

## Testing an edit here

- For a quick loop on an edit of the checker or the code generator, compile the edited class into a scratch directory, and run the compiler with that directory first on its class path. This takes seconds, rebuilds nothing and changes nothing tracked. Give each run a fresh copy of the caches, because nothing checks the caches against the compiler that wrote them, and a compile of an unchanged program with a jar writes nothing:

      Q=$PWD/tmp/quick ; export FORTRESS_CACHES=$Q/caches ; CP=$(bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1)
      mkdir -p $Q/classes && javac -nowarn -cp "$CP" -d $Q/classes ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/<path>/X.java
      rm -rf $Q/caches && cp -a default_repository/caches $Q/caches
      java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -Dfortress.caches=$Q/caches -cp "$Q/classes:$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell compile P.fss
      bin/fortress run P

  For a Scala file, compile it with `java -cp "$CP" scala.tools.nsc.Main -classpath "$CP" -d $Q/classes -encoding UTF-8 X.scala`. Then put the edit into the tree and build it for real.
- If your change is near transactions, top-level mutable state or the class loader's first load, do the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`).

## The checker's time

This section is for a change of the checker: its Scala under `scala_src/`, or `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast` and the generators under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/`, from which the build generates the checker's syntax tree and `Walker`.

The count stage takes `<out-file> <scratch>` and about 150 seconds, more under load. That is longer than the Bash tool's default time limit, so run it in the background (`session.md`). It writes a table to the out-file: the errors of each api, the total, the number of places with errors, and the first crash. It keeps the checker's whole output in `<scratch>/run.txt`, and its caches in `<scratch>`, so a run from the base build leaves the base build as it was.

The checker checks every api first, and the component only if no api has an error. In each api or component, it stops at the first of its stages that finds errors. The stages run in this order (`compiler/StaticChecker.java`, `checkCompilationUnit`):

1. The type hierarchy and the type check.
2. The overloading check, which also compares the overloads' return types.
3. In the component only, the export check (`library.md`, "Designing a change").

So the count misses the errors of the later stages, and a fix of an early error can raise it.

The table's rows tell a clean run from a run that the checker did not finish:

content.content:
Each path has its own library today. At the switch-over, the compiled path moves onto the interpreter's library, and the compiler's prelude, three files of its library, is deleted (`references/compiler.md`). The compiled checker already finds no error in the interpreter's library. For the `FortressLibrary` component, the count stage shows this as a total of 0 (`references/compiler.md`). The switch-over waits for walk's natives: each function that the interpreter's library binds with `builtinPrimitive` (`references/interpreter.md`, "Natives") must first have a binding that the compiled path runs.

- **Dispatch is on every argument, at run time.** A call chooses among overloads by the run-time types of all its arguments, as in Julia, not by static types as in Java. The checker accepts two overloads only if their parameter types exclude each other, one is strictly more specific, or a third covers their meet. The more specific one's return type must fit the other's. Walk checks part of this at load.
- **Functional methods.** A method with `self` among its parameters is called `f(x)`, not `x.f()`. It overloads with top-level functions. Most operators are declared so: `opr +(self, other: T): T`. A functional method's name is reserved in every program that imports it, so do not name a variable after it. One type must not have a dotted and a functional method of the same name.
- **Traits and objects, no classes.** A trait has methods and abstract fields, and extends several traits. An object is a leaf. `excludes {A, B}` says that no value has both types. `comprises {A, B}` says that every value has a listed type, near Scala's `sealed`. No type may extend two instantiations of one generic trait. This exclusion rule is why the number types are flat (below).
- **Static parameters.** They are written `[\T\]`, and `[i]` indexes. Their kinds are types, sizes (`nat` is an `NN32` value, `int` a `ZZ32`), `bool` and `opr`. Generics are invariant: there is no `+T` or `-T`. An unbounded type parameter is bounded by `Any`, which holds tuples, functions and `()`, as `Object` does not. A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound. Under walk, one whose bound names the parameter itself stays open, and every value passes it. Walk instantiates a reduction or a comprehension without static arguments at the type declared for its value: a local variable's type, or a top-level or local function's return type. Without one, it uses the join, the least common supertype, of its elements' run-time types. Some other cases still get the empty type `Bottom` under walk (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Static parameters").
- **Numbers are siblings, not a tower.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`. None is a subtype of another, unlike Haskell's classes or Java's widening. A wider type declares a `coerce` from each narrower one. A conversion never changes which declaration runs when one already fits. Overflow raises `IntegerOverflow`. The algebra is self-typed traits, such as `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` with `+`, not monoids over an operator parameter. `references/library.md` gives the rest: ranges, wrapping, `SUM`.
- **Loops and reductions are library code.** `for`, comprehensions and `SUM` call the library's generators and reductions (`references/library.md`).
- **Juxtaposition is an operator, and whitespace counts.** `f x` applies a function. Otherwise juxtaposition is an operator that the library overloads: `2 x` multiplies, and `"a" "b"` concatenates. How three juxtaposed items group depends on their types, unlike in Haskell. An infix operator has whitespace on both sides or on neither: `a -b` is a static error. Precedence is partial: `a + b ∪ c` needs parentheses.
- **Specified, but not built:** dimensions and units, `property` declarations, regions and complex numbers. Some constructs run only under walk (`references/compiler.md`).

content.content:
- two declarations of one name that its parameter-by-parameter check cannot order. It accepts them if `comprises` clauses cover the overlap. For every pair of functions of which at least one is generic, it checks the overloading rules of `SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language", on their declared domains (`revival-changes.md`, "Dispatch and overloading"): the No Duplicates Rule, the Meet Rule and the Return Type Rule. So it refuses two whose declared domains are equal. The message names the rule: "fails because their parameter lists have the same types", "fails the Return Type Rule" or "fails the Meet Rule". Walk keeps the team's check and messages for the pairs below. The team's check looks for
  - a pair with a varargs parameter;
  - a pair whose parameter lists differ in length, only where one of them has a varargs parameter. Walk checks no other pair of lists of different lengths;
  - a pair that is neither two generic declarations nor a generic one beside a plain one;
  - the instances of an explicit instantiation.

  Where it reads exclusion over the whole tuple of parameter types, at the instance that the equalities force, it reads two parameter types that still mention a static parameter as excluding only where no instances of the two can meet. Walk departs from the rules in these cases:
  - At load, it does not check two functional methods of a generic trait or object on their declared domains. It compares them at each call, on the instance that the call makes. So such a pair that breaks the rules loads, and a call can fail with "Cannot find definition for method" (ledger row 780).
  - It refuses two generic functional methods whose declared domains lie one inside the other, in a type without static parameters (ledger row 779).
  - It refuses a pair whose overlap it finds only through an instance of a supertype, also where a third declaration covers the overlap (ledger row 539).
  - It refuses overloads on two instantiations of one generic type, as `g(b: Tg[\3\])` beside `g(b: Tg[\4\])` (ledger row 416).
  - Its parameter-by-parameter check reads an object type over a static parameter as excluding a type that one of its instances is or extends. So it loads `g[\T\](x: Box[\T\], y: ZZ32)` beside `g(x: Box[\ZZ32\], y: Any)`, which the Meet Rule refuses (ledger row 788).
  - It reads no `where` clause when it reads exclusion over the whole tuple. So it refuses such a pair where one declaration has a `where` clause of its own (ledger row 787).
  - Where a program's own component declares both, it refuses a generic operator between an array of a number type and a number, on either side, beside the operator of a self-typed trait, as `AdditiveGroup`'s `+`: "at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types". The checker accepts such a pair, and the library's own pairs load (ledger row 804).
  - It loads a function over `Index` beside one over a pair whose element types neither lie below `Index` nor exclude it, which the Meet Rule refuses (ledger row 806).
  - It loads a type that provides two functional symbolic operators, such as two `||`, that break the Meet Rule for Functional Methods (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`). The checker refuses the pair (ledger row 611).

  The paths differ on `f[\T extends { K, R[\T\] }\](x: T)` beside `f(x: Z)`, where `K comprises { A, B, C }`, `Z excludes { A, B }`, and `C` is an object that extends `Z` but not `R`. Walk refuses the pair: "fails the Meet Rule". The checker reads the bounds, finds that no value lies in both domains, and accepts it. No decision says which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 713).
- two functional methods that break the Meet Rule for Functional Methods in a type that provides both, where their name is an identifier or an operator named by a word, as `MAX`.
- an overloaded function with one parameter of type `T`, where `T extends Any` is written: `f[\T extends Any\](x: T)`.
- an extender that a `comprises` clause of the program's main component does not allow. Walk does not yet check the library's clauses, another component's clauses or an object expression's clauses. Where a listed type names a bounded type `where`-clause variable, as `NBox[\E\]` in `comprises { NBox[\E\] } where [\E extends Number\]`, walk ignores the variable's bound, and runs `NBox[\String\]` (ledger row 754). In another declaration's bound, it takes a name equal to the variable's as the variable (ledger row 778).
- a trait whose `comprises` clause lists a type at a `where`-clause variable, where a member's declared type names the variable: "Missing type E" (ledger row 755).
- an object or object expression without static parameters that inherits an abstract method and does not define it. Bodies define it if they are at or below its parameter types and together cover them, with `comprises` clauses read. Walk also refuses where its search for a cover does not settle: at a cycle of `comprises` clauses, at a symbolic type, or beyond 10,000 steps or 4,096 combinations of listed types. It also refuses a valid object whose one body for the method has a static parameter of its own (ledger row 728).
- a declaration with the modifier `override`, in a trait, object or object expression, that overrides no declaration that its type's immediate supertraits provide. An `override` at an inherited declaration's own parameter types overrides nothing. At an instance of a generic trait above a declared object, equal parameter types count as overridden. Walk does not read all the bounds of the static parameters in two cases:
  - an object expression, which takes its static parameters from the function around it;
  - a generic trait or object that extends a type under a `where` clause.

  In these cases, walk does not refuse an `override` if the inherited declaration's parameter types mention a static parameter and differ from the `override`'s.

So a library edit can stop every program at load, if it does one of these:

- adds an overload;
- leaves an inherited abstract method that no bodies cover, covers it only by a body with a static parameter of its own, or covers it by bodies whose cover walk's search cannot settle;
- adds an `override` that overrides nothing;
- gives a member a type that names its trait's `comprises`-clause variable, as `E` in `AnyList`.

Walk checks a program's declarations against the library's only when it analyses the library, not when it loads the library's entries from the cache (ledger row 342). So a program that walk refuses with an empty cache runs with a filled one. Deleting the program's own entries does not bring the check back. To see such a refusal, run with an empty cache, as `COLD_CACHE=1` gives `harness-one.sh`.

`tests-writing.md` says how a test names a refusal at load.

Walk's overload-ambiguity message names its two declarations in an order that varies from run to run. On one core, the order is fixed for a given library, but a library edit can change it. Do not pin or compare this order. The harness reads only that an `XXX` test fails.

content.content:
**checker count**
: Errors that the compiled checker reports on the interpreter's library, up to each component's first error.

**distance**
: All the compiled checker's errors on the interpreter's library, which must reach zero before the switch-over, the move of the compiled path onto the interpreter's library. The gate's distance stage counts them (`explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh`), and FACTS holds the current value.

## The go

- The batches of PLAN's phase 3 run on a standing go, in PLAN's order. Launch each when the batch before it has landed and its own batch record has no open question.
- If a question that the batch record raises is consequential (`SKILL.md`), put it to the curator first. Otherwise decide it and put it on the review list. While the curator is away, overnight, take its recommended default and put it on the review list. If that default would reverse a decision of the curator, hold that batch, and launch the repair batch (`explorations/coordinator/REPAIR-BATCH.md`) in its place.
- Have one Fable review read each coming batch record before the launch, with a go in advance. It is written for the curator in place of reading the record. Treat its questions as the batch record's.

## The workflow

- Between batches, improve the script and the manual where a batch showed a problem.
- Let every step spend the fewest workers that it needs.
- Build the base once, yourself, in a worktree where nobody compiles or runs (`args.baseBuild`). Every rung worktree is seeded from it (`explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh`), never built clean.
- No stage runs a build, a suite or a measurement again on a code state that another stage ran, and no agent reads again a log that has not changed.
- Let the planner give each rung its mission briefing, from the territory map (`explorations/coordinator/map/`), in neutral words: "the decisions on record", not the curator's name. Require no answers from the worker about how it searched.
- At each landing, report the share of briefed agents that read the briefing at all. Aim for all of them. By the brief's order, none reads it in its first turn.

## The roles

- The skeptic checks a rung's result after its worker, and builds nothing to check. It reads from the worker's transcript whether the test came first and failed. It runs its own small programs on the rung's build, and on the base through `explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh` with a private caches folder. Where the rung changes the compiled checker, the skeptic also runs the count stage itself, on the base build and on the worker's commits, as `fortress-repo`'s `compiler.md`, "The checker's time", gives a reviewer. That run is the one exception to this bullet and to the rule that no stage measures a code state again.
- It checks the result against the library's way, the ledger, sibling sites and the decisions on record, and fixes what it finds, test first.
- A judge rules only on a fix that the skeptic marks contested, on a rung that the skeptic refuses, or on a rung whose worker reported that it could not go on. The first ruling runs on Opus, a second on Fable (`judgeTier`). A settled fix lands with the review and the gate as its check. Reaching a reserved point, or a file outside what the rung's section of the batch record names, does not make a settled fix contested: it lands, and the point or the file goes on the review list. A point that cannot be undone holds the batch.
- No batch compares the printed outputs of the suites' test programs, and no baseline is run to compare against.

## The checker count and the distance

The gate reports the checker count in every batch, and the distance in phase 3. Neither turns the gate red.

- If a rung's test is the checker count or the distance, it takes the last landed gate's tables as its starting values.
- If every file that a rung changes lies outside what the two measures read, the rung runs neither and lists those files (`STAGE_BLIND`). Its skeptic checks the list against the branch's diff.
- The review after the batch ties every new or risen row of the count's table to a named rung edit.
- The gate's comparisons hide Java line numbers, identity hashes and moved library positions. Put every difference that they hid on the review list. Put there too each line of the team's tests that a rung rewrote to keep its checked value, with its before and after.

## Reserved points and repairs

- A reversible reserved point does not hold the batch. The batch lands with the point's default, and the point goes on the review list.
- An output that the base already varies from run to run, with the test's verdict unchanged, is a ledger row.
- After its one repair round, a merged-diff review that still blocks does not hold a batch whose gate is green. Its findings go on the review list, for the batch after. The review runs once in each batch.
- A repair after the gate runs the gate again only if it changes what the gate reads (its part in `fortress-repo`).
- If the gate over a merged batch is red, do not bisect. Find the cause as a whole, and rework that part in the merged batch. If the gate is still red after its repair, the batch does not land: put it to the curator at once, as a hold.

## While it runs

- At a boot, read the batch record's sections for the curator, the run's journal (`references/delegating.md`) at the run ID in the check-in file (below), and the times of its agents' transcripts in the session's `subagents/workflows/<run>/`.
- From the launch until the run ends, by landing, by stopping or by holding its push for the curator, edit no tracked file in the main tree, the boot note included. The gather needs `git status --porcelain` there to print nothing. Push nothing to `main` from any tree, or git refuses the landing's push.
- Before the launch, name the check-in file in the boot note: `<scratchpad>/batch<N>/checkins.txt`, where `<N>` is the batch's number. After the launch, write the run's ID and each armed check-in's ID in that file. If the scratchpad loses a check-in's ID, find the check-in again with `list_triggers`.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# skill-load.py [--repo DIR] RUN_DIR [RUN_DIR...]
#
# The measure the earlier transcript studies lacked (explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/skill-effect.md):
# per agent of a Workflow run, the calls that load a skill and the parts of .claude/skills/ it reads.
# RUN_DIR is a run's directory (<project>/<session>/subagents/workflows/wf_<id>/: one agent-<id>.jsonl and
# agent-<id>.meta.json per agent, the label in the meta file's "description"), as for tools/batch-measures.py.
# Nothing is run; the transcripts are only read.
#
#   writes:     input plus cache-creation tokens, each message counted once by its id (labor.md's method).
#   loads:      tool calls named Skill, with the skill's name; "load text" is the text the harness injects after
#               such a call (a user message that opens "Base directory for this skill:"), in characters and in
#               tokens at labor.md's 0.40 a character.
#   parts read: Bash, Read, Grep and Glob calls that name a file under .claude/skills/: SKILL.md or a
#               references/ part. A part is a *.md name that exists in .claude/skills/ in some commit of the
#               repository's history (git log --all), so that a skill's older parts count too. A Bash call that
#               enters a skills folder (cd) and then names parts relative to it counts for those parts. A call that
#               names no part (ls, grep -r) counts as "(search of skills)". The result of a call is charged
#               0.40 tokens a character plus 110 (labor.md), shared equally between the parts the call names.
#   brief:      whether the agent's first message names the skill (the word fortress-repo).

# Committing and pushing

**scratch**
: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.

Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.

## What to commit

- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.

## How to commit

Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:

    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>

- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB

  If your brief gives another session line, use it.

## Pushing

Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.

- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
  3. If it lists only your commits, push three times, in this order:

         git push origin main
         git push origin main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8
         git push origin main:blinded-fable

     The third push keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and say so in your report.
